Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3") or SHA1 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3") or MD5 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3") or SHA1 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3") or MD5 in~ ("a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a90c3433006cdedfbb135718f309209c0699cb097d4a55e85357130d5ec689b3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Trojanized wermgr.exe spawning SYSTEM command shell — RoguePlanet privilege escalation · [LLM] Devices exposed to RoguePlanet — Malware Protection Engine below 1.1.26060.3008 (CVE-2026-50656)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Microsoft Defender engine (MsMpEng.exe) overwriting System32\wermgr.exe — RoguePlanet CVE-2026-50656
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Microsoft Defender engine (MsMpEng.exe) overwriting System32\wermgr.exe — RoguePlanet CVE-2026-50656 AIInstallation High
Hunts the core RoguePlanet privilege-escalation primitive: the Defender scanning engine (MsMpEng.exe) winning a TOCTOU race and writing/replacing C:\Windows\System32\wermgr.exe with the attacker payload. The Defender engine legitimately quarantines to its own store and never writes an executable into System32, so this is a near-zero-baseline exploitation signal. Rationale: Uses the exact exploit primitive corroborated by external write-ups: the Defender engine binary MsMpEng.exe writing into C:\Windows\System32\wermgr.exe. Both the writing process and the target path are fixed, article-specific values with effectively no legitimate occurrence. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-patches-rogueplanet-defender.html • https://www.morphisec.com/blog/microsoft-defender-zero-day-rogueplanet-when-your-detector-becomes-the-attack-surface/ • https://threatprotect.qualys.com/2026/06/18/microsoft-defender-zero-day-vulnerability-exploited-in-attacks-cve-2026-50656-rogueplanet/
ATT&CKT1068 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Defender legitimately flagging a genuinely-infected wermgr.exe and quarantining it (write would target the quarantine store, not overwrite System32 — verify FolderPath)
  • Windows feature/servicing update replacing wermgr.exe via TiWorker.exe/TrustedInstaller (parent would NOT be MsMpEng.exe)
  • Security researcher / red-team validating the PoC in a lab
  • EDR file-event path normalization mislabeling the initiating process during a Defender platform update
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "Quarantine" and FolderPath !has "Windows Defender"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is MsMpEng.exe and the target is literally C:\Windows\System32\wermgr.exe (not the quarantine path); pull SHA256 of the new wermgr.exe and compare to the Microsoft-signed baseline. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any wermgr.exe-spawned SYSTEM shells, and restore the legitimate signed wermgr.exe; verify Malware Protection Engine is >= 1.1.26060.3008. 3) Hunt: search the host for wermgr.exe spawning cmd/powershell (UC2), manual triggers of the Windows Error Reporting scheduled task, and other System32 binaries recently written by MsMpEng.exe.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "wermgr.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\System32\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "MsMpEng.exe"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "wermgr.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\System32\"
| where ActingProcessName has "MsMpEng.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Defender Engine Overwrites System32 wermgr.exe (RoguePlanet CVE-2026-50656)
id: 8f3c1a42-7b6e-4d29-9c0a-2e6b1f4a9d11
description: MsMpEng.exe (Microsoft Malware Protection Engine) writing to System32\wermgr.exe indicates abuse of the CVE-2026-50656 remediation race condition.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/microsoft/microsoft-patches-rogueplanet-defender-zero-day-vulnerability/
  - https://www.morphisec.com/blog/microsoft-defender-zero-day-rogueplanet-when-your-detector-becomes-the-attack-surface/

  - attack.t1036.005

  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\MsMpEng.exe'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\System32\wermgr.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\MsMpEng.exe OR *\\msmpeng.exe OR *\\MSMPENG.EXE) @TargetFilename:(*\\System32\\wermgr.exe OR *\\System32\\WERMGR.EXE OR *\\system32\\wermgr.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/MsMpEng\.exe$/i TargetFileName=/wermgr\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="wermgr.exe" Filesystem.file_path="*\\System32\\wermgr.exe" Filesystem.process_name="MsMpEng.exe" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="wermgr.exe" Filesystem.file_path="*\\System32\\wermgr.exe" Filesystem.process_name="MsMpEng.exe" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Trojanized wermgr.exe spawning SYSTEM command shell — RoguePlanet privilege escalation AIExploitation High
Hunts the RoguePlanet payoff: the overwritten C:\Windows\System32\wermgr.exe (executed via the Windows Error Reporting scheduled task) spawning cmd.exe/powershell.exe as SYSTEM. Legitimate wermgr.exe handles Windows Error Reporting and launches WerFault, never an interactive shell. Rationale: Anchors on the concrete post-exploitation behavior confirmed across sources: System32 wermgr.exe (the WER handler) launching an interactive SYSTEM shell. The parent binary and its System32 path are fixed article-specific values; legitimate wermgr.exe never spawns cmd/powershell. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-patches-rogueplanet-defender.html • https://www.rescana.com/post/cve-2026-50656-microsoft-defender-rogueplanet-zero-day-enables-local-privilege-escalation-on-fully-patched-windows-10-11 • https://www.morphisec.com/blog/microsoft-defender-zero-day-rogueplanet-when-your-detector-becomes-the-attack-surface/
ATT&CKT1068 T1053.005 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/debug session where wermgr.exe is manually invoked to inspect Windows Error Reporting (extremely rare)
  • Third-party crash-reporting tooling renaming its own binary to wermgr.exe (verify signature/path)
  • Red-team or PoC validation of RoguePlanet in a lab
  • EDR mis-parenting where conhost or a task engine is collapsed into wermgr.exe as parent
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "-queue" and Grandparent in~ ("svchost.exe","taskhostw.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm ParentImage is System32\wermgr.exe and the child shell runs at SYSTEM/High integrity; capture the child command line and the wermgr.exe SHA256. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the SYSTEM shell and any children, and snapshot for forensics before restoring the signed wermgr.exe. 3) Hunt: correlate back to UC1 (MsMpEng.exe writing wermgr.exe) on the same host, review scheduled-task run history for Microsoft-Windows-WER, and sweep for lateral movement or credential dumping performed under the SYSTEM shell.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "wermgr.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\System32\"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessIntegrityLevel, Grandparent = InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\wermgr.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TokenElevationType, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Devices exposed to RoguePlanet — Malware Protection Engine below 1.1.26060.3008 (CVE-2026-50656) AIExploitation High
Posture hunt that surfaces endpoints still exposed to CVE-2026-50656 because their Microsoft Malware Protection Engine (mpengine.dll) has not yet reached the fixed build 1.1.26060.3008. Because the fix ships via automatic engine update rather than Patch Tuesday, SOC needs explicit visibility into laggards. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-50656) and the concrete fixed engine build (1.1.26060.3008) named in the article and confirmed by vendor coverage; TVM exposure listing is the cleanest way to enumerate unpatched engine versions. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/microsoft-patches-rogueplanet-defender.html • https://securityaffairs.com/195016/security/microsoft-fixed-defender-flaw-rogueplanet-cve-2026-50656.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/09/microsoft-releases-fix-for-rogueplanet-defender-flaw-cve-2026-50656/
ATT&CKT1068
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Devices already auto-updated to 1.1.26060.3008 but TVM inventory not yet refreshed (transient, clears within a day)
  • Offline/dormant endpoints that legitimately haven't pulled the engine update yet
  • Air-gapped hosts pending manual engine definition delivery
  • Non-Windows or Defender-uninstalled hosts appearing with stale inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each listed device confirm current Malware Protection Engine version and whether it is below 1.1.26060.3008 (1.1.26050.11 or earlier = vulnerable). 2) Contain: force a Defender security-intelligence/engine update on exposed hosts and prioritize internet-facing and high-privilege endpoints. 3) Hunt: on any host that stayed vulnerable for an extended window, run UC1 and UC2 retrospectively to rule out RoguePlanet exploitation before the engine was updated.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-50656"
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-50656"
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50656")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-50656")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Poisoned repo drop: security.sh + disguised 'code_policies' Go binary on host
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] AI coding agent (Claude Code / Codex) executing README-suggested security.sh · [LLM] AI coding agent executes a repo-local binary during autonomous review (Friendly Fire port) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Top AI Agents Built to Catch Malicious Code Can Be Tricked Into Running It
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Disguised 'code_policies' payload binary executed (masquerades as Go build) · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Poisoned repo drop: security.sh + disguised 'code_policies' Go binary on host AIDelivery High
Hunts the delivery step of the AI Now 'Friendly Fire' PoC: a third-party library that ships a security.sh wrapper alongside a pre-compiled 'code_policies' payload binary disguised as the build of a co-located code_policies.go decoy. Fires on creation of these specific artifacts (e.g. during git clone/checkout) before any AI agent runs them. Rationale: Anchors on the exact artifact names from the PoC repo (security.sh, code_policies, code_policies.go) confirmed by both the AI Now brief and the Boyan-MILANOV GitHub repo — code_policies/.go are near-unique strings, giving high fidelity for the drop before execution. Cross-checked against: • https://ainowinstitute.org/publications/friendly-fire-exploit-brief • https://github.com/Boyan-MILANOV/friendly-fire-ai-agent-exploit • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cyber-ai-agents-hijacked/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate project that genuinely ships a helper file named security.sh (a fairly common CI/security-scan script name)
  • A researcher cloning the public stripped-payload PoC repo for reproduction
  • A Go project that legitimately contains a package/file named code_policies.go
  • Developer authoring their own security.sh linting wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("friendly-fire-ai-agent-exploit") and FileName == "code_policies.go")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect FolderPath/InitiatingProcess — confirm the write came from git/clone into an untrusted third-party repo and that a co-located code_policies binary (no extension, ELF/PE) sits beside code_policies.go. Hash the binary and check prevalence/VT. 2) Contain: quarantine the repo directory, block the code_policies SHA256, and prevent any AI coding agent from being pointed at that folder in auto mode. 3) Hunt: pivot on DeviceProcessEvents for any execution of security.sh or code_policies on the host (UCs below) and for other repos on the same dev box carrying an unreferenced compiled binary next to a same-named .go source.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName in~ ("security.sh","code_policies","code_policies.go","code_policies.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("security.sh","code_policies","code_policies.go","code_policies.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI coding agent (Claude Code / Codex) executing README-suggested security.sh AIExploitation High
Core Friendly Fire detection: an AI coding agent process (claude/codex/node) spawns the security.sh wrapper or the code_policies payload while auto-reviewing untrusted code — the agent runs a script that only a README told it to run, with no user approval. Parent-process pivot on the agent binary makes this a security-tool-executes-unexpected-code signal. Rationale: Combines the article's named artifacts (security.sh, code_policies) with the AI-agent parent process (claude/codex/node) — the exact 'the agent executing a binary or script that only a README told it to run' behaviour the researchers flag as the clearest thing to watch for. Cross-checked against: • https://ainowinstitute.org/publications/friendly-fire-exploit-brief • https://github.com/Boyan-MILANOV/friendly-fire-ai-agent-exploit
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher deliberately reproducing the (stripped) PoC with Claude Code / Codex
  • A legitimate repo whose own build/test flow the agent runs that happens to invoke a file named security.sh
  • Developer manually running security.sh in a shell that was itself launched by the agent's terminal integration
  • Internal tooling named code_policies used sanctioned in the org
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "friendly-fire-ai-agent-exploit" and AccountName !in~ ("secresearch","redteam")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm InitiatingProcessFileName is a real AI agent (claude/codex/node running the CLI) and that the target repo is untrusted third-party code, not an internal project; capture the code_policies SHA256 and FolderPath. 2) Contain: kill the agent process, isolate the host, block the binary hash, and disable auto-mode/auto-review for that workspace. 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents from the code_policies process and its descendants for any egress (PoC stops at exec, but a real port may add C2), and sweep other dev endpoints for the same agent-parent → security.sh chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "security.sh" or ProcessCommandLine has "code_policies" or FileName in~ ("code_policies","code_policies.exe"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude","claude.exe","codex","codex.exe","node","node.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetProcessCommandLine has "security.sh" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "code_policies" or TargetProcessName has "code_policies")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("claude","codex","node")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Disguised 'code_policies' payload binary executed (masquerades as Go build) AIInstallation High
Fires on execution of the code_policies binary — the Friendly Fire payload carrier disguised as the compiled build of a co-located code_policies.go, seeded with strings lifted from that source so the agent's disassembly check ties them together. Surfaces the payload process, its hash, and parent (security.sh/shell) for IOC pivoting regardless of which agent launched it. Rationale: code_policies is the near-unique payload-binary name confirmed by the PoC repo; the masquerade (a compiled binary disguised as the build of code_policies.go, string-seeded to fool disassembly) is the defense-evasion crux, so any execution of it is high-fidelity and yields the hash for blocking. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/Boyan-MILANOV/friendly-fire-ai-agent-exploit • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cyber-ai-agents-hijacked/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1027 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate static-analysis tool genuinely named code_policies in the environment
  • Security team reproducing the public PoC (payload stripped) for validation
  • A build system compiling code_policies.go into a same-named binary in a sanctioned internal project
  • EDR sample-detonation of the artifact in a sandbox VM
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "friendly-fire-ai-agent-exploit" and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the code_policies SHA256/MD5 and FolderPath; confirm parent is security.sh/a shell under an AI agent and that no repo source actually references the binary (the tell — nothing calls it). 2) Contain: block the hash org-wide, isolate the host, and terminate the process tree. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts that have ever written or run code_policies, review child processes and outbound connections for post-exec activity, and check whether any secrets/keys on the dev host were accessed during the process lifetime.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "code_policies" or ProcessCommandLine has "code_policies" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "code_policies"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "code_policies" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "code_policies" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "code_policies"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, Hash, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI coding agent executes a repo-local binary during autonomous review (Friendly Fire port) AIExploitation Medium
Behavioral generalization of Friendly Fire for real-world ports that rename the artifacts: an AI coding agent (claude/codex) in auto mode executes a compiled binary living inside a user code/repo directory that is not a standard toolchain interpreter — i.e. running a payload that only the repo's docs pointed it to. Hunting-tier because it drops the specific PoC names in favor of the behaviour. Rationale: The researchers say the payload ports to almost any project with different filenames, so this drops the PoC-specific names and keys on the invariant: an AI coding agent auto-executing a non-toolchain compiled binary from within an untrusted repo tree — the durable behaviour behind Friendly Fire. Cross-checked against: • https://ainowinstitute.org/publications/friendly-fire-exploit-brief • https://www.nxcode.io/resources/news/friendly-fire-rogue-agent-ai-coding-security-2026
ATT&CKT1059 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Agent legitimately running a project binary it just built (e.g. ./myapp, ./target/release/app) as part of a requested build-and-run task
  • Repo-local test harness or fuzzer binaries invoked by the agent during sanctioned work
  • Language servers or linters shipped inside a repo's tools/ directory
  • Monorepo task-runner binaries executed from the workspace root
  • Developer-blessed helper executables in Downloads used during triage
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("go build","cargo build","npm run build","make ") or FolderPath has_any (@"\target\release\", @"\target\debug\", @"\dist\", @"\build\", "/target/release/", "/dist/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the executed binary's SHA256, prevalence, and whether any repo source references it; confirm the agent was in auto-mode reviewing untrusted third-party code rather than building a trusted project. 2) Contain: if unrecognized/low-prevalence, isolate the host, block the hash, and switch the affected workspace to approve-before-run. 3) Hunt: baseline which binaries each agent normally executes per user, alert on first-seen repo-local executables, and correlate with README/docs files added in the same repo that instruct running a checker/script.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude","claude.exe","codex","codex.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Documents\", @"\repos\", @"\projects\", @"\src\", "/home/", "/Users/", "/tmp/")
| where FileName !in~ ("node","node.exe","npm","npm.cmd","git","git.exe","python","python3","python.exe","pip","pip3","go","cargo","rustc","tsc","jest","pytest","bash","bash.exe","sh","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","pwsh","powershell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("claude","codex")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("Downloads","Documents","repos","projects","/home/","/Users/","/tmp/","src")
| where not(TargetProcessName has_any ("node","npm","git","python","pip","cargo","rustc","tsc","jest","pytest","bash","sh","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\claude.exe OR *\\Claude.exe OR *\\codex.exe OR *\\Codex.exe) @Image:(*\\Downloads\\* OR *\\Documents\\* OR *\\repos\\* OR *\\projects\\* OR *\\src\\*) -@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\npm.cmd OR *\\git.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\pip.exe OR *\\go.exe OR *\\cargo.exe OR *\\bash.exe OR *\\sh.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(claude|codex)(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(Downloads|Documents|repos|projects|src|tmp)(\\|\/)/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/(node|npm|git|python[0-9]?|pip[0-9]?|go|cargo|rustc|tsc|jest|pytest|bash|sh|dash|zsh|cmd|powershell|pwsh)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

falsepositives:

level: high

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39861")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-39861")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-39861")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-39861")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process_name IN ("security.sh"))
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name,
       Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| append [
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified")
      AND (Filesystem.file_name IN ("security.sh"))
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name,
       Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
]
Critical

GhostApproval Symlink Flaws Could Let Malicious Repos Run Code in AI Coding Agents

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 11 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Researchers at&nbsp;Wiz&nbsp;found that a flaw in six popular AI coding assistants lets a booby-trapped code project quietly take control of a developer's computer. The assistant asks permission to edit one harmless-looking file, but the write lands on a sensitive one instead. The affected tools are Amazon Q Developer, Anthropic's Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf.

AI coding agent writes SSH authorized_keys or shell rc via GhostApproval symlink AIInstallation High
Hunts the GhostApproval payload landing: an AI coding assistant process (Amazon Q, Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Augment, Antigravity) creating or modifying ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or a shell startup file (~/.zshrc, ~/.bashrc, ~/.profile) because a repo symlink named like a benign config file (project_settings.json) resolved to the sensitive target. This is the write that grants password-less SSH or arbitrary command execution on the next terminal. Rationale: Anchored on the exact GhostApproval targets confirmed by Wiz (~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.zshrc) and the six named agent processes; the pairing of a sensitive Unix dotfile write with an AI-agent initiating process is the specific, high-fidelity signal the article describes. Cross-checked Wiz blog and AWS bulletin. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/ghostapproval-a-trust-boundary-gap-in-ai-coding-assistants • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/2026-047-aws/
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1546.004 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • nvm / oh-my-zsh / starship installers spawned via node appending to ~/.zshrc during legit setup
  • A developer intentionally letting an agent add its own SSH key to authorized_keys for a remote dev container
  • Dotfile-manager tooling (chezmoi, yadm) launched from an IDE-embedded terminal running under node
  • Python-based provisioning scripts (Ansible local, pip post-install hooks) editing ~/.bashrc
  • IDE 'shell integration' features writing rc-file hooks on first launch
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("oh-my-zsh","nvm.sh","chezmoi","yadm","starship init") and FileName in~ (".zshrc",".bashrc"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the parent repo path; open the target file and diff — a foreign ssh-rsa/ed25519 key in authorized_keys or an exported command / curl|bash line in .zshrc confirms it. Check whether the workspace was a freshly cloned/untrusted repo. 2) CONTAIN: Remove the injected key/line, rotate any exposed SSH keys, revoke the developer's active sessions, and quarantine the repo. If SSH is internet-reachable, block the host at the firewall until cleaned. 3) HUNT: Search all endpoints for the same agent process writing dotfiles; pivot to remote SSH logons on the host after the write and to any .amazonq/mcp.json in the repo.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName == "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh/")
    or FileName in~ (".zshrc",".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshenv",".zprofile",".zlogin")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","code","Code.exe","cursor","Cursor","cursor.exe","windsurf","Windsurf","windsurf.exe","claude","antigravity","augment","python","python3")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("amazonq","amazon-q","language-server","cursor","windsurf","claude","augment","antigravity")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ssh-keygen","sshd"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (TargetFileName == "authorized_keys" and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh/")
    or TargetFileName in~ (".zshrc",".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshenv",".zprofile",".zlogin")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","code","cursor","windsurf","claude","antigravity","augment")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("amazonq","language-server","cursor","windsurf","claude","augment","antigravity")
| where ActingProcessName !has "ssh-keygen"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AI Coding Agent Writes SSH authorized_keys or Shell RC (GhostApproval)
id: 8f2c1a94-6b7e-4d21-9c3a-1e5f2a7b0c11
status: experimental
description: Detects an AI coding assistant process modifying ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or a shell startup file, the GhostApproval symlink payload landing.

Amazon Q / AI agent spawns shell child from poisoned .amazonq/mcp.json (CVE-2026-12957) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts CVE-2026-12957: a poisoned repo ships an .amazonq/mcp.json (or equivalent agent config) that Amazon Q auto-loads once the workspace is trusted, launching MCP-server processes that inherit the developer's AWS keys and can run commands. Detects an AI agent / language-server process spawning a shell or interpreter child that runs credential-touching commands (curl, chmod, base64, reads of ~/.aws). Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit CVE-2026-12957 detail (poisoned repo auto-loads a config file .amazonq/mcp.json and runs commands to steal AWS keys) plus the six named agent parents; requires the agent->shell->credential-command chain rather than bare agent-spawns-node so it stays hunting-grade. Cross-checked AWS bulletin 2026-047 and Wiz. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/2026-047-aws/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/amazon-q-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1195.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate MCP server defined by a trusted repo shelling out to curl/pip during normal setup
  • Language-server post-install hooks running python/base64 for packaging
  • Developer-authored VS Code tasks that chmod +x build scripts
  • AI agent legitimately fetching a dependency via curl during a user-approved build
  • CI-runner style repos where node spawns bash for test bootstrap
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/build/","npm run","pytest","pip install") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","npm") and not ProcessCommandLine has_any (".aws/credentials","authorized_keys"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full ProcessCommandLine of the shell child and inspect the repo for .amazonq/mcp.json (or similar agent config) with an unexpected 'command'/'args'. Confirm whether ~/.aws/credentials was read or exfiltrated (network egress from the child). 2) CONTAIN: Kill the spawned process tree, rotate the developer's AWS keys and any cloud CLI tokens immediately, and revoke sessions. Update Amazon Q Language Server to >=1.69.0. 3) HUNT: Enumerate repos on the host for agent config files (.amazonq/mcp.json, mcp.json), review DeviceNetworkEvents from the agent for uploads to unfamiliar hosts, and check for the SSH-key / dotfile writes from the companion UCs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","code","Code.exe","cursor","Cursor","cursor.exe","windsurf","Windsurf","windsurf.exe","claude","antigravity","augment")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("amazonq","amazon-q","language-server",".amazonq/mcp.json","mcp.json")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","zsh","dash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","python","python3","osascript")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","chmod","base64",".aws/credentials",".aws\\credentials","authorized_keys","aws_access_key")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "mcp.json"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","code","cursor","windsurf","claude","antigravity","augment")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("amazonq","language-server","mcp.json")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("bash","/sh","zsh","dash","cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","python","osascript")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","chmod","base64",".aws/credentials","authorized_keys","aws_access_key")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has "mcp.json"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node","node.exe","code","Code.exe","cursor","windsurf","claude","antigravity","augment") OR Processes.parent_process="*amazonq*" OR Processes.parent_process="*mcp.json*" OR Processes.parent_process="*language-server*") AND (Processes.process_name IN ("bash","sh","zsh","dash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","python","python3","osascript")) AND (Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*" OR Processes.process="*chmod*" OR Processes.process="*base64*" OR Processes.process="*.aws*" OR Processes.process="*authorized_keys*" OR Processes.parent_process="*mcp.json*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
SSH authorized_keys planted then remote SSH logon (GhostApproval key-injection use) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Temporal correlation that catches the payoff of the GhostApproval SSH variant: ~/.ssh/authorized_keys is created/modified on a host, then a successful remote (network/SSH) logon occurs on the same host within an hour using the freshly planted key. Distinguishes a benign key add from an attacker immediately logging in. Rationale: Chains the two article-confirmed facts (agent writes into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, then 'they can log in with no password') into a time-window correlation so it only fires when the planted key is actually used remotely - far tighter than alerting on every authorized_keys edit. Corroborated by Wiz PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/ghostapproval-a-trust-boundary-gap-in-ai-coding-assistants
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1021.004 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin adds a legitimate key then immediately SSHes in to validate access
  • Configuration-management (Ansible/Salt) pushing authorized_keys followed by a scripted SSH health check
  • Cloud-init / provisioning that installs a key then the orchestrator connects
  • Jump-host onboarding where a new key and first login happen back to back
  • Backup/CI service accounts rotating keys and reconnecting
Suppression filter
| where KeyWriter !in~ ("sshd","cloud-init","ansible","salt-minion","puppet","cfn-init")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the process that wrote authorized_keys is an AI agent (KeyWriter field) rather than sshd/cloud-init/config-mgmt, and check whether the RemoteIP of the logon is expected for that user. 2) CONTAIN: If unexpected, kill the SSH session, remove the injected key, rotate credentials, and block the source IP; isolate the host if the repo is confirmed malicious. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the RemoteIP across the fleet for other SSH logons, review commands run in the session, and search other hosts for the same agent writing authorized_keys or .zshrc.
let win = 1h;
let keyWrites = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where FileName == "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh/"
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
    | project KeyWriteTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where LogonType in ("Network","RemoteInteractive") or Protocol =~ "Ssh"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| join kind=inner keyWrites on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (KeyWriteTime .. KeyWriteTime + win)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, KeyWriteTime)
| project KeyWriteTime, LogonTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, RemoteIP, DelaySec, KeyWriter = InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LogonTime desc
let win = 1h;
let keyWrites = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where TargetFileName == "authorized_keys" and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh/"
    | where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
    | project KeyWriteTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ProcessName == "sshd" and SyslogMessage has "Accepted publickey"
| join kind=inner keyWrites on $left.Computer == $right.DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (KeyWriteTime .. KeyWriteTime + win)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, KeyWriteTime)
| project KeyWriteTime, LogonTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, SyslogMessage, DelaySec, ActingProcessName
| order by LogonTime desc
source:linux.syslog @process.name:sshd "Accepted publickey"
#event_simpleName=UserLogon
| RemoteAddressIP4=*
| LogonType=/(3|10)/
| join({#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\/\.ssh\/authorized_keys$/i | rename(ContextImageFileName, as=KeyWriter)}, field=aid, include=[KeyWriter])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, RemoteAddressIP4, KeyWriter], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as KeyWriteTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="authorized_keys" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/*" AND (Filesystem.action=created OR Filesystem.action=modified) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | join type=inner dest [| tstats `summariesonly` min(_time) as LogonTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success AND (Authentication.app="sshd" OR Authentication.signature="ssh") by Authentication.dest Authentication.src Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`] | where LogonTime >= KeyWriteTime AND LogonTime <= KeyWriteTime+3600 | eval DelaySec=LogonTime-KeyWriteTime | convert ctime(KeyWriteTime) ctime(LogonTime) | table dest process_name KeyWriteTime LogonTime DelaySec src user
| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as KeyWriteTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="authorized_keys" AND Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/*" AND (Filesystem.action=created OR Filesystem.action=modified) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | join type=inner dest [| tstats summariesonly=false min(_time) as LogonTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success AND (Authentication.app="sshd" OR Authentication.signature="ssh") by Authentication.dest Authentication.src Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`] | where LogonTime >= KeyWriteTime AND LogonTime <= KeyWriteTime+3600 | eval DelaySec=LogonTime-KeyWriteTime | convert ctime(KeyWriteTime) ctime(LogonTime) | table dest process_name KeyWriteTime LogonTime DelaySec src user
Symlink created in repo pointing to SSH/AWS/shell files (GhostApproval staging) AIWeaponization Low
Hunts the GhostApproval staging step: creation of a symbolic link (ln -s, mklink, New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink) whose link name masquerades as a benign project file (e.g. project_settings.json) but whose target is a sensitive out-of-repo path (~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.zshrc, ~/.aws/credentials, /etc). Catches attacker/CI/manual symlink planting; note git-checkout creates symlinks via syscall and is not covered by process telemetry. Rationale: Anchored on the exact PoC command Wiz published (ln -s ~/.ssh/authorized_keys project_settings.json) and the confirmed sensitive targets; requires the symlink target to be a sensitive out-of-repo path so it does not fire on ordinary symlinks. Low confidence flagged because git checkout plants symlinks via syscall (not ln) and won't appear here - it complements, not replaces, the file-write UC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/ghostapproval-a-trust-boundary-gap-in-ai-coding-assistants
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dotfile managers (chezmoi, stow, yadm) that symlink ~/.zshrc or ~/.ssh/config into a managed repo
  • Developer manually symlinking a shared .env or config into a project
  • Build scripts that symlink /etc/localtime or CA bundles into a container context
  • Homebrew/Nix post-install linking into the user profile
  • Test fixtures that create relative parent-traversal symlinks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("chezmoi","stow","yadm","nix","brew") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Resolve the symlink target vs its name (readlink) and confirm the link name looks like an in-repo config (e.g. *.json/.env) while the target is a sensitive dotfile - a mismatch is the GhostApproval tell. Check the repo origin/trust. 2) CONTAIN: Delete the symlink before any agent 'sets up' the repo, and if an agent already ran, inspect the target file for injected content and remediate per the SSH/rc UC. 3) HUNT: Grep the repo tree for other symlinks resolving outside the workspace, and search the fleet for the same repo/URL and for agent processes writing authorized_keys/.zshrc.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "ln" and ProcessCommandLine has "-s")
    or (FileName in~ ("cmd.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "mklink")
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh") and ProcessCommandLine has "SymbolicLink")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("authorized_keys","/.ssh",".zshrc",".bashrc",".bash_profile",".aws","/etc/","System32","..\\..","../..")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (TargetProcessName endswith "/ln" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "-s")
    or (TargetProcessName has "cmd.exe" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "mklink")
    or (TargetProcessName has_any ("powershell","pwsh") and TargetProcessCommandLine has "SymbolicLink")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("authorized_keys","/.ssh",".zshrc",".bashrc",".aws","/etc/","System32","..\\..","../..")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Symlink Created Pointing to SSH/AWS/Shell Files (GhostApproval Staging)
id: 4a71e2c5-0d3b-4f19-a6c2-7b8e9f014d22
status: experimental
description: Detects creation of a symbolic link whose target is a sensitive out-of-repo path, the GhostApproval symlink staging step.
references:
    - https://www.wiz.io/blog/ghostapproval-a-trust-boundary-gap-in-ai-coding-assistants
    - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ghostapproval-symlink-flaws-could-let.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/09
tags:
    - attack.defense_evasion
    - attack.t1036.005
    - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: linux
detection:
    selection_ln:
        Image|endswith: '/ln'
        CommandLine|contains: '-s'
    selection_target:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'authorized_keys'
            - '/.ssh'
            - '.zshrc'
            - '.bashrc'
            - '.aws'
            - '/etc/'
    condition: selection_ln and selection_target
falsepositives:
    - Dotfile managers or setup scripts that symlink ~/.zshrc or ~/.ssh/config into a repo intentionally
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:ln AND @process.command_line:*"-s"* AND @process.command_line:(*authorized_keys* OR *.zshrc* OR *.bashrc* OR *.ssh* OR *.aws* OR */etc/*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\/ln$/i
| regex("\\s-s(\\s|f)", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(authorized_keys|/\\.ssh|\\.zshrc|\\.bashrc|\\.aws|/etc/|System32|\\.\\.)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="ln" AND Processes.process="*-s*") OR (Processes.process="*mklink*") OR (Processes.process="*SymbolicLink*")) AND (Processes.process="*authorized_keys*" OR Processes.process="*/.ssh*" OR Processes.process="*.zshrc*" OR Processes.process="*.bashrc*" OR Processes.process="*.aws*" OR Processes.process="*/etc/*" OR Processes.process="*System32*" OR Processes.process="*..*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="ln" AND Processes.process="*-s*") OR (Processes.process="*mklink*") OR (Processes.process="*SymbolicLink*")) AND (Processes.process="*authorized_keys*" OR Processes.process="*/.ssh*" OR Processes.process="*.zshrc*" OR Processes.process="*.bashrc*" OR Processes.process="*.aws*" OR Processes.process="*/etc/*" OR Processes.process="*System32*" OR Processes.process="*..*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

DeviceFileEvents

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-12958", "CVE-2026-50549", "CVE-2026-12957")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-12958", "CVE-2026-50549", "CVE-2026-12957")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-12958", "CVE-2026-50549", "CVE-2026-12957")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-12958", "CVE-2026-50549", "CVE-2026-12957")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'

Fake 7-Zip Installers Turn Devices Into Residential Proxy Nodes

The Hacker News
2026-07-09 12 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new threat actor dubbed Lurking Lizard that has been operating an end-to-end malicious residential proxy business using an infrastructure comprising more than 230 lookalike domains. The activity dates back to at least August 2022, according to DNS threat intelligence firm Infoblox. Once such campaign, observed earlier this year, involved the

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Lurking Lizard proxyware lookalike distribution/proxy-brand domain resolution · [LLM] Fake installer (7-Zip/WhatsApp/WireVPN) written to disk from Lurking Lizard domain
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanized 7-Zip/WireVPN installer spawning command interpreter or LOLBin · Suspicious browser extension installation

Lurking Lizard proxyware lookalike distribution/proxy-brand domain resolution AIDelivery High
Hunts DNS resolution and network connections to the Lurking Lizard lookalike domains used to distribute trojanized 7-Zip/WhatsApp/WireVPN installers and to impersonate proxy brands. Article-specific because it pins the exact drop-catch/typosquat domains (7zip.com vs 7-zip.org, whtatsapp.net, wirevpn.*) rather than a generic newly-registered-domain heuristic. Rationale: Uses the exact Infoblox-published typosquat/drop-catch domains (7zip.com not 7-zip.org, whtatsapp.net, wirevpn.app/.cc/.io) plus the impersonated proxy-brand domains — a fixed IOC list, so any resolution is high-fidelity rather than a generic NRD heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/fake-installers-fake-reviews-fake-services-real-proxies-real-victims/ • https://gbhackers.com/lurking-lizard-uses-drop-catch-domains/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/lurking-lizard-uses-fake-7-zip-installers/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or threat-intel analyst detonating/browsing the reported domains from a sandbox VM
  • URL-detonation or web-crawler appliance fetching the domains for reputation scoring
  • User genuinely searching for '911proxy'/'smartproxy' proxy services and landing on the lookalike storefront
  • DNS sinkhole/passive-DNS collector resolving the domains as part of enrichment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on DeviceName/src — was resolution followed by an .exe/.msi download from the same host? Check InitiatingProcessFileName (browser vs. non-browser). 2) Contain: block the domains at DNS/proxy, isolate the host if a non-browser process resolved them or an installer was written. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for the same domains, check for iplogger.com/mnWD beacons and /client_v1/* proxy check-ins (UC2/UC3), and enumerate installers dropped from these hosts.

IPLogger tracking beacon (iplogger.com/mnWD) from non-browser process AICommand & Control High
Hunts the hardcoded IPLogger tracking link (iplogger.com/mnWD) embedded in the Lurking Lizard fake-installer samples, contacted by a non-browser process. Article-specific: this exact IPLogger short-URL is the single artifact Infoblox used to tie the 7-Zip, TikTok/YouTube-downloader and WireVPN samples to the same actor. Rationale: iplogger.com/mnWD is the specific tracking artifact Infoblox names as the pivot linking every fake-installer variant to Lurking Lizard; contact from a non-browser process is a strong proxyware-beacon signal, and the /mnWD path (in proxy/web logs) makes it campaign-unique rather than generic IPLogger noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/fake-installers-fake-reviews-fake-services-real-proxies-real-victims/ • https://gbhackers.com/lurking-lizard-uses-drop-catch-domains/
ATT&CKT1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate marketing/analytics use of IPLogger by an internal user clicking a tracked link in a browser (excluded by the non-browser filter)
  • Security tooling detonating a sample and following the embedded IPLogger link
  • Chat/IM client following a user-pasted iplogger.com link
  • Threat-intel enrichment service resolving iplogger.com for reputation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is not a browser and inspect its folder path (Downloads/Temp/AppData) and parent — a fresh installer beaconing to IPLogger is the trojanized dropper. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture the beaconing binary + hash, block iplogger.com/mnWD at proxy. 3) Hunt: pull the binary's other network destinations (proxy /client_v1/* endpoints, UC3), check autoruns/scheduled tasks for persistence, and search the org for the same SHA256.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl contains "iplogger.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","safari.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "iplogger.com/mnWD" or DstHostname =~ "iplogger.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, HttpMethod, Url, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
