Residential-proxy client check-in to /client_v1/config/http and /client_v1/version/server AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Lurking Lizard proxyware client's HTTP check-in to its config/version API endpoints, which Infoblox found shared identical schemas across the campaign's domains. Article-specific: these exact URI paths are the proxy client's C2/registration channel that turns the host into an exit node. Rationale: The /client_v1/config/http and /client_v1/version/server paths are the campaign-specific API schema Infoblox observed across multiple Lurking Lizard domains — an unusual, non-standard URI pair unlikely to collide with legitimate traffic. Datadog/Falcon left blank because HTTP URI paths are not reliably present in Sysmon-only or FDR EDR telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/fake-installers-fake-reviews-fake-services-real-proxies-real-victims/ • https://gbhackers.com/lurking-lizard-uses-drop-catch-domains/
ATT&CKT1090 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal API that happens to expose a /client_v1/version/server versioning path (verify destination host is external/untrusted)
  • Web-app pentest or fuzzing traffic hitting versioned API paths
  • Vulnerability scanner probing common API routes
  • Proxy log parsing that URL-decodes and matches a similarly named path on a trusted SaaS host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination host is external and matches (or resolves like) the Lurking Lizard lookalike infra; identify the source process/host and its install origin. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the destination and the /client_v1/* paths at proxy, kill/quarantine the proxy client binary. 3) Hunt: this host is likely an active exit node — review outbound volume for third-party proxied traffic, correlate with the iplogger beacon (UC2) and installer drop (UC4), and sweep peers for the same URI paths.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/client_v1/config/http","/client_v1/version/server")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any ("/client_v1/config/http","/client_v1/version/server")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, HttpMethod, Url, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake installer (7-Zip/WhatsApp/WireVPN) written to disk from Lurking Lizard domain AIDelivery High
Hunts an executable/MSI installer written to disk whose download origin is a Lurking Lizard lookalike domain, catching the trojanized 7-Zip/WhatsApp/WireVPN/Snaptik installer at the delivery step. Article-specific via the concrete distribution domains plus the impersonated product names. Rationale: Combines the named distribution domains with an executable/MSI file-origin — Defender's FileOriginUrl ties the dropped installer directly to the actor's infra. Sigma/Datadog/Falcon blank: the FileOriginUrl-to-file correlation has no clean single-event Sigma shape and no FDR/Sysmon file-origin equivalent, so Splunk/Sentinel use the web-download view instead. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/fake-installers-fake-reviews-fake-services-real-proxies-real-victims/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/lurking-lizard-uses-fake-7-zip-installers/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst intentionally downloading a sample from the reported domain for analysis
  • URL-rewrite/email-security gateway pre-fetching a linked installer
  • Browser 'download and scan' feature retrieving the file into a sandbox
  • Web proxy caching an .exe from the flagged host during content inspection
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the dropped file SHA256 and confirm it is NOT the legitimate Igor Pavlov 7-Zip (compare against official 7-zip.org hashes); check if it was executed. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block the origin domain, isolate the host if the installer ran. 3) Hunt: if executed, look for the IPLogger beacon (UC2), the /client_v1/* proxy check-in (UC3) and child-process spawns (UC5); sweep the org for the same SHA256 and origin domains.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileOriginUrl has_any ("7zip.com","whtatsapp.net","wirevpn.app","wirevpn.cc","wirevpn.io","snaptik.io","isharkvpn.com","betflixfree.net")
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".msi"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession

| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, FileName, DstIpAddr, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized 7-Zip/WireVPN installer spawning command interpreter or LOLBin AIInstallation Low
Behavioral hunt for a 7-Zip/WireVPN/Snaptik installer-named parent process spawning cmd/PowerShell/mshta/rundll32/regsvr32/wscript — the execution of the hidden proxy payload bundled in the trojanized installer. Legitimate 7-Zip (7z/7zFM/7zG) rarely spawns interpreters, making this a useful low-noise pivot. Rationale: Anchors on the article's installer product names (7-Zip, WireVPN, Snaptik, iSharkVPN) as the parent and standard interpreters/LOLBins as the child; genuine 7-Zip archive tools almost never spawn these, so the parent-child pair is the intent signal. Low confidence because the article does not name the specific payload binary, so this is a hunting pivot rather than a hard IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/fake-installers-fake-reviews-fake-services-real-proxies-real-victims/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/lurking-lizard-uses-fake-7-zip-installers/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 7-Zip SFX/self-extracting archive that runs a bundled setup.cmd/install script
  • Software packaging or IT deployment wrapping 7-Zip to launch cmd/PowerShell post-extract
  • WhatsApp desktop updater spawning a helper process
  • A build/CI agent using 7z.exe in a pipeline that then calls cmd.exe
  • Legitimate WireVPN client (if org uses one) invoking rundll32 for driver setup
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\") and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("MpCmdRun","DismHost","choco"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line for download/execution (curl/certutil/bitsadmin, base64, or connections) and confirm the parent is a downloaded installer, not a signed 7-zip.org build. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the installer + child artifacts, capture hashes. 3) Hunt: verify network for iplogger.com/mnWD (UC2) and /client_v1/* proxy check-ins (UC3), check Run keys/Scheduled Tasks for persistence of the proxy client, and sweep peers for the same parent binary hash.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("7z","7zip","7-zip","wirevpn","snaptik","isharkvpn","whatsapp")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("7z","7zip","7-zip","wirevpn","snaptik","isharkvpn","whatsapp")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256

      - '\7zFM.exe'
      - '\7zG.exe'
      - '\7zip.exe'
      - '\wirevpn.exe'
      - '\snaptik.exe'
      - '\isharkvpn.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
      - '\regsvr32.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\7z.exe OR *\\7zFM.exe OR *\\7zG.exe OR *\\7zip.exe OR *\\wirevpn.exe OR *\\WireVPN.exe OR *\\snaptik.exe OR *\\isharkvpn.exe) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.EXE OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(7z|7zFM|7zG|7zip|7-zip|wirevpn|snaptik|isharkvpn).*\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|wscript|cscript|curl|bitsadmin|certutil)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("7z.exe","7zFM.exe","7zG.exe","7zip.exe","7-zip.exe","wirevpn.exe","snaptik.exe","isharkvpn.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*7-zip*setup*" OR Processes.parent_process="*wirevpn*setup*" OR Processes.parent_process="*snaptik*setup*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("7z.exe","7zFM.exe","7zG.exe","7zip.exe","7-zip.exe","wirevpn.exe","snaptik.exe","isharkvpn.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*7-zip*setup*" OR Processes.parent_process="*wirevpn*setup*" OR Processes.parent_process="*snaptik*setup*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")

          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName

| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'

            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows

    selection_psexec:

            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:

level: high

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.

Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("7zip.com", "whtatsapp.net", "wirevpn.app", "wirevpn.cc", "wirevpn.io", "betflixfree.net", "isharkvpn.com", "snaptik.io", "bintangwarisanhotel.com", "proxyreviews.org")

ImNetworkSession

   or Url has_any (BadDomains)

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain

Symlinks Are Still Scary (And Yes, You Can Commit Them to Git)

Snyk
2026-07-09 5 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A harmless-looking symlink in a Git repo can redirect a tool into reading or writing anywhere on your machine. That old trick is now showing up in AI coding assistants, with nasty results.

SSH authorized_keys written by non-SSH tooling (symlink repo payload) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts writes/modifications to any user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys where the writing process is NOT legitimate SSH provisioning tooling — the payoff of the article's headline attack, where a symlink named like project_settings.json checked out from a cloned repo resolves to authorized_keys and a build script/editor/AI coding agent silently writes an attacker key through it. Because the OS resolves the symlink transparently, the file event reports the real target path (.ssh/authorized_keys), which is the tell. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact payload path ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (code Block 1) written by non-SSH tooling — the symlink resolves so the OS reports the real target, making the write-through observable. Cross-checked MITRE T1098.004, Splunk Security Content and Elastic authorized_keys rules to confirm the technique and avoid duplicating a generic FIM rule by scoping on the writing process. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/004/ • https://research.splunk.com/endpoint/f5ab595e-28e5-4327-8077-5008ba97c850/ • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/cross-platform/persistence_ssh_authorized_keys_modification
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible/Puppet/Salt/Terraform pushing authorized_keys via a config-management run (excluded, but custom wrappers may slip through)
  • Developer legitimately running ssh-copy-id or manually editing authorized_keys with vim/nano
  • Cloud-init / provisioning agent seeding keys on first boot of a new VM
  • CI runner injecting a deploy key into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as an intended step
  • Dotfile-management tools (chezmoi, GNU stow) that symlink or template SSH config
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("terraform","authorized_keys_command","chezmoi","stow") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ansible"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess chain — is the writer a dev tool (git, node, python, code, cursor) or shell spawned from a freshly cloned repo path? Compare the written key fingerprint against the user's known keys and check if the file is/was a symlink (ls -l ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, readlink). 2) Contain: if the key is unrecognized, remove the offending authorized_keys line, kill active sessions authenticated by it, and rotate the account; quarantine the source repo. 3) Hunt: search the same host/user for the source symlink (git ls-files -s | grep '^120000'), other writes to ~/.ssh, ~/.bashrc, ~/.git/hooks, and any inbound SSH logons using the added key.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath endswith "/.ssh/authorized_keys" or (FileName == "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sshd","ssh","ssh-keygen","ssh-copy-id","cloud-init","useradd","adduser","ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFilePath endswith "/.ssh/authorized_keys" or (TargetFileName == "authorized_keys" and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRename")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("sshd","ssh-keygen","ssh-copy-id","cloud-init","ansible","puppet","salt-minion"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SSH authorized_keys Written by Non-SSH Tooling (Symlink Repo Payload)
id: 5c2e6b1a-9f3d-4a77-8b0e-2d1c6f9a4e21
description: Detects creation or modification of a user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys by a process that is not legitimate SSH provisioning tooling, consistent with a symlink committed to a cloned git repository resolving to authorized_keys and being written through by a build script, editor, or AI coding agent.
references:
  - https://snyk.io/blog/symlinks-are-still-scary/
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/004/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:
  - attack.t1098.004
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '/.ssh/authorized_keys'
  filter_legit:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sshd'
      - '/ssh-keygen'
      - '/ssh-copy-id'
      - '/cloud-init'
      - '/ansible'
      - '/salt-minion'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*authorized_keys* AND (*">>"* OR *tee* OR *">"*)) -@process.executable.path:(*/sshd OR */ssh-keygen OR */ssh-copy-id OR */cloud-init)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\/\.ssh\/authorized_keys$/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\/(sshd|ssh-keygen|ssh-copy-id|cloud-init)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*/.ssh/authorized_keys" Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified","renamed") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action Filesystem.process_guid

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Git-spawned hook execution during recursive clone (CVE-2024-32002) AIExploitation High
Hunts a process whose image lives inside a .git/hooks/ directory and whose parent is git — the exact signature of CVE-2024-32002, where a malicious repository's crafted submodule + symlink writes a hook into .git/ that git executes while the clone is still running, yielding RCE from nothing more than git clone --recurse-submodules. No build step or 'run the project' required. Rationale: Anchored on the CVE-2024-32002 mechanic named in the article (git clone --recurse-submodules dropping a script into .git/hooks and running it during clone). The parent=git + child-image-in-.git/hooks pair is high-fidelity because hooks are not supposed to execute during a clone; confirmed via the git security advisory GHSA-8h77-4q3w-gfgv and Amal Murali's PoC writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/git/git/security/advisories/GHSA-8h77-4q3w-gfgv • https://amalmurali.me/posts/git-rce/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2024/05/16/git-cve-2024-32002/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer with legitimately installed local git hooks (post-checkout/post-merge) firing during a normal pull or checkout
  • Husky / pre-commit framework hooks that shell out during commit or checkout operations
  • CI systems that intentionally invoke repo hooks as part of a pipeline stage
  • git-lfs post-checkout smudge hooks running on a large-file repo clone
  • Monorepo tooling (e.g. Nx, Turborepo) that registers checkout hooks
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("husky","git-lfs","post-merge") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pull","checkout HEAD","lfs"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the executed hook file under .git/hooks/ and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm it was a clone/--recurse-submodules op and read the hook body for network callbacks or key writes. Check git version on host against the patched set (>=2.39.4/2.40.2/2.41.1/2.42.2/2.43.4/2.44.1/2.45.1). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the hook process tree, and quarantine the cloned repo directory; block the source repo URL. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for downstream child processes of the hook, writes to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, new persistence (cron, systemd units, shell rc files), and outbound C2 from the hook's PID.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.git/hooks/", "\\.git\\hooks\\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","git.exe","git-remote-https","git-remote-https.exe","bash","sh","dash")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","submodule","--recurse-submodules") or FolderPath has_any ("post-checkout","post-clone","post-update")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/.git/hooks/", "\\.git\\hooks\\")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("git","bash","sh","dash")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","submodule","--recurse-submodules") or ActingProcessName has_any ("post-checkout","post-clone","post-update")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joro proxy-mode confused-deputy: browser POSTs to loopback API 127.0.0.1:9090 (CVE-2026-53649) AIDelivery Low
Hunts a web browser process opening connections to the Joro proxy-mode API on loopback TCP/9090, the confused-deputy vector CVE-2026-53649 abuses when attacker-controlled cross-origin JavaScript reaches the unauthenticated, wildcard-CORS Joro API. Article-specific because it pins the exact bind (127.0.0.1:9090) and the browser-mediated initiator. Rationale: Uses the exact loopback bind (127.0.0.1:9090) named in the advisory plus a browser-process initiator, the confused-deputy shape of CVE-2026-53649. Deliberately hunting/Low because a legitimate Joro operator's own browser talks to the same UI/API port. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling • https://github.com/bishopfox
ATT&CKT1189 T1204.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Joro operator using the proxy-mode web UI, which itself talks to 127.0.0.1:9090
  • Unrelated local dev services on 9090 (Prometheus Pushgateway, SonarQube, custom app) that a browser hits
  • Browser DevTools/extension polling a localhost dev server on the same port
  • Local reverse-proxy or API mock bound to 9090 during development
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Joro is installed/running on the host and whether the operator was actively using the Joro UI at that timestamp; pull the browser history for the immediately preceding external navigation. 2) Contain: if the loopback hit was NOT operator-initiated UI use, kill the joro process, isolate the host, and block the external page's domain at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot to whether joro subsequently wrote a .so plugin, restarted, or spawned an interactive shell (see companion UCs) — that sequence confirms exploitation.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP

Joro native plugin RCE: joro process spawns interactive /bin/bash shell (CVE-2026-53649) AIExploitation High
Alerts when the joro binary spawns an interactive Unix shell (bash/sh/dash/zsh with -i), the terminal step of the CVE-2026-53649 chain where a malicious uploaded plugin's init() opens a goroutine and yields an interactive /bin/bash -i shell as the operator's user. High fidelity because joro is a proxy/teamserver, not a shell launcher — it has no legitimate reason to fork a local login shell. Rationale: Pins the article's exact parent (joro) and payload (interactive /bin/bash -i obtained on plugin.Open() init()). Because Joro is a proxy that never legitimately forks a local login shell, parent=joro + shell + -i is a near-zero-FP RCE tell. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.004 T1129
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Joro developer/operator debugging the tool and manually shelling out from a plugin during testing
  • A local wrapper or helper script also named 'joro' that legitimately invokes a shell
  • Operator running a benign self-authored plugin that spawns a shell for tooling
  • CI/build harness building Joro plugins that exec a shell as part of a test
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child shell's full process tree and any sockets it holds (ss -p); confirm the joro process previously loaded a newly-written .so and restarted. 2) Contain: kill the shell and joro process, isolate the host, and snapshot /proc for the joro PID before termination for the loaded-plugin path. 3) Hunt: enumerate the Joro plugin directory for attacker-uploaded .so files, review recent POSTs to /api/v1/plugins/upload and /api/v1/system/restart, and check outbound connections from joro to external hosts.

Joro writes a native .so plugin: attacker plugin drop before restart (CVE-2026-53649) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the joro process writing a shared-object (.so) plugin file to disk, the staging step where CVE-2026-53649's unauthenticated upload endpoint persists an attacker-supplied native plugin that executes its init() on the next plugin.Open(). Article-specific via the joro-process writer plus the .so plugin artifact. Rationale: Ties the article's plugin-upload artifact (a native .so consumed by plugin.Open()) to the joro process as writer. joro dropping a .so it did not build interactively is the on-disk footprint of the upload endpoint being abused. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling
ATT&CKT1129 T1203

  • Operator legitimately installing/updating a Joro plugin through the intended workflow
  • Joro's own --build-plugin feature emitting a compiled .so during plugin development
  • Package manager or updater refreshing bundled Joro plugins on the same host
  • Backup/sync tooling restoring the Joro plugin directory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the written .so, submit to sandbox/AV, and check whether it was preceded by a browser hit to 127.0.0.1:9090 and a joro restart. 2) Contain: quarantine the .so, stop joro before it re-opens the plugin, and isolate the host if the file is unsigned/unknown. 3) Hunt: look for joro spawning an interactive shell or making outbound public connections after the write, and sweep other operator hosts for the same .so hash (one ABI-matched plugin works against every operator on the release).

Nuclio CronJob curl shell-injection reading Kubernetes serviceaccount token AIExploitation High
Hunts a /bin/sh -c curl invocation (as built by the Nuclio controller for cron triggers) whose command line both reads the pod serviceaccount token and contains shell metacharacters, indicating exploitation of CVE-2026-52831 header-key/body command injection. Article-specific because it pins on the exact curl --header shape plus the /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token read shown in the PoC. Rationale: Anchors on the exact PoC artefacts: a curl --header command line (the controller's generated sink) that also reads /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, plus shell metacharacters ($(, ;, &&) that only appear when Path-A/Path-B injection breaks the quoting context.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator running kubectl exec into a pod and using curl -H with the serviceaccount token to test the Kubernetes API
  • Legitimate in-cluster script that curls the API server with a custom header whose value contains '; charset=utf-8'
  • CIS-benchmark / security scanner tooling that reads the serviceaccount token path
  • CI/CD sidecar that reads the token and curls an internal admission endpoint
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine contains "; charset=" or ProcessCommandLine contains ";q=" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "kubectl")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and confirm the injected fragment (text after the closing quote of --header, or a $(...) in the echoed body); map the host/pod to the owning NuclioFunction and cron trigger. 2) Contain: suspend/delete the offending CronJob (kubectl delete cronjob), delete the NuclioFunction, and rotate the pod serviceaccount token / bound token if it was read. 3) Hunt: enumerate all CronJobs in the nuclio namespace lacking ownerReferences, review other functions' cron trigger event.headers/event.body for metacharacters, and pivot on outbound connections from the same pod (UC5).

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has "--header"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("$(", ")", "`", ";", "&&")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--header"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("$(", ")", "`", ";", "&&")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Egress from Nuclio CronJob curl process reading serviceaccount token to public IP AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a curl process that read the serviceaccount token (the injected command) with an outbound connection to a non-private IP within a short window — the token/secret exfiltration step of CVE-2026-52831 RCE. Multi-stage correlation on the same host/pod. Rationale: Ties the injected token-reading curl (from UC1) to a public egress within 5 minutes — the exfiltration shape of the RCE. Uses the exact token path and curl process; RFC1918 exclusion isolates external destinations. CIM Network_Traffic field names may need site-local mapping. Empty CloudWatch/Sigma (multi-stage, non-AWS).
ATT&CKT1020 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Function legitimately curls an external webhook/API as its designed behaviour
  • Cron trigger intentionally targeting a public endpoint
  • Egress through a NAT/CDN/proxy destination that looks public
  • Outbound telemetry from a sidecar that also happens to read the token
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl endswith ".svc.cluster.local" or RemoteIP startswith "100.64.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the same host/pod both read the serviceaccount token and made the external connection; resolve the destination IP/URL and check reputation. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress, kill the CronJob/pod, and rotate the serviceaccount token and any secrets the pod could reach. 3) Hunt: pull all destinations contacted by curl processes on nuclio pods, look for repeated beaconing to the same external IP, and cross-reference UC4 for downstream API abuse with the stolen token.
let TokenReads = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)

    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("$(", ")", "`", ";", "&&")
    | project TokenReadTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Install of fake Paysafe/Skrill/Neteller npm & PyPI credential-stealer packages AIInstallation High
Hunts developer/CI machines running npm or pip against the 17 named malicious payment-SDK packages (paysafe-*, skrill*, neteller) that impersonate legitimate Paysafe/Skrill/Neteller SDKs and steal API keys, AWS keys, GitHub and npm tokens. Article-specific because it keys on the exact package names published in this campaign, not generic dependency installs. Rationale: Uses the 17 exact package names Socket enumerated (paysafe-checkout, paysafe-vault, skrill-sdk, neteller, etc.) scoped to the actual package-manager binaries — high fidelity because these package names have no legitimate publisher and installation is the campaign's install step. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher intentionally detonating the packages in a sandbox to reproduce the campaign
  • An internal private-registry package that legitimately contains the substring 'skrill' or 'paysafe' in its name
  • A blue-team engineer running an IOC-validation install against a proxy that blocks the fetch
  • A dependency-audit tool that references the package names in a lockfile scan (not an actual install)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--registry=https://your-internal-registry" and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the exact package + version installed (npm 1.0.0-1.0.3 or PyPI 1.0.0 are the malicious ranges) and identify the machine/CI runner and user. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner and immediately rotate ALL secrets present on that machine — Paysafe API keys, AWS keys, GitHub tokens, npm tokens — per Socket's guidance. Deny the package names at the registry proxy. Step 3 (hunt): Search dependency trees org-wide for any of the 17 names, grep CI logs for PAYSAFE_API_KEY appearing alongside these package names, and pivot to UC2 to check for outbound exfil to the ngrok C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm","node.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("paysafe-checkout","paysafe-vault","paysafe-js","paysafe-api","paysafe-node","paysafe-cards","paysafe-fraud","paysafe-kyc","paysafe-payments","paysafe-sdk","skrill-payments","skrill-sdk","skrill","neteller")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","add"," i ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("npm","node.exe","pip","python","yarn","pnpm")
| where CommandLine has_any ("paysafe-checkout","paysafe-vault","paysafe-js","paysafe-api","paysafe-node","paysafe-cards","paysafe-fraud","paysafe-kyc","paysafe-payments","paysafe-sdk","skrill-payments","skrill-sdk","skrill","neteller")
| where CommandLine has_any ("install","add")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 exfil to Paysafe-stealer ngrok endpoint caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev AICommand & Control High
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to the campaign's exfiltration endpoint caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev, the C2 the fake payment SDKs POST stolen credentials/tokens to. Article-specific because it keys on the single confirmed IOC domain from this campaign rather than the whole ngrok TLD. Rationale: Keys on the single confirmed IOC domain (caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev) from the article — a direct match is nearly always malicious since it is the stealer's dedicated exfil endpoint, giving very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A malware analyst or threat-intel researcher deliberately resolving the IOC for enrichment
  • A DNS sinkhole/RPZ that logs the query before blocking it (query still appears in DNS telemetry)
  • Passive DNS collectors or scanning tools crawling the ngrok subdomain
  • The ngrok free subdomain being recycled to a benign tunnel by a different user after takedown
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the host and the initiating process — correlate the connecting process (Node/Python) with UC1 to confirm one of the 17 malicious packages ran on this machine. Step 2 (contain): Block caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat all secrets on it as compromised — rotate Paysafe API keys, AWS keys, GitHub and npm tokens immediately. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep proxy/DNS logs org-wide for the same domain over 30d, review AWS CloudTrail for any use of exfiltrated AWS keys from unfamiliar IPs, and check GitHub/npm audit logs for token misuse.

| where RemoteUrl has "caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b") or SHA1 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b") or MD5 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b") or SHA1 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b") or MD5 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

High

AI Coding Agents Found Triggering Endpoint Security Rules Built to Catch Attackers

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Sophos looked at a week of its own endpoint data and found that AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenAI Codex are setting off detection rules written to catch human intruders. The agents are not malicious. They just do a lot of things that, to a behavioral engine, look exactly like an attack. Decrypting browser credentials, listing what sits in Windows' credential store,

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] certutil-blocked-then-bitsadmin LOLBin download pivot on same host
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Claude Code launched with --dangerously-skip-permissions guardrail bypass · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — AI Coding Agents Found Triggering Endpoint Security Rules Built to Catch Attacke
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Startup-folder script drop via PowerShell (Cursor persistence pattern) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DPAPI browser-credential decrypt via PowerShell (GStack /browse skill under AI coding agent) · [LLM] Windows Credential Manager enumeration via cmdkey /list under coding agent · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
DPAPI browser-credential decrypt via PowerShell (GStack /browse skill under AI coding agent) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact PowerShell one-liner GStack's /browse skill runs under Claude Code/Cursor to unlock Chromium credential data: Add-Type System.Security then ProtectedData::Unprotect on a base64 blob. Detects browser-credential decryption regardless of whether an AI agent or an attacker drove it, while surfacing the agent parent for triage. Rationale: Uses the verbatim GStack /browse command signature from the Sophos blog (ProtectedData::Unprotect + FromBase64String under powershell), which is the highest-fidelity string in the article; the AgentLineage tag distinguishes benign agent automation from real theft without dropping either. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer's Claude Code running GStack /browse for legitimate browser automation
  • Password managers or browser-profile migration utilities that legitimately DPAPI-decrypt saved logins
  • Authorized red-team/pentest tooling exercising browser credential extraction
  • Security research or QA reproducing the Sophos finding
  • Backup/sync tooling re-protecting DPAPI blobs on the same user context
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and InitiatingProcessParentFileName — if the parent is claude.exe/cursor.exe/codex it is likely benign agent automation; confirm the logged-on user actually runs a coding agent. 2) Contain: if the parent is NOT a known agent (real theft), isolate the host and force-reset the browser-stored credentials and any SSO sessions decrypted. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for cmdkey /list, certutil/bitsadmin downloads, and startup-folder writes within the same session to separate agent noise from an intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData"
    and ProcessCommandLine has "Unprotect"
    and ProcessCommandLine has "FromBase64String"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend AgentLineage = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe","node.exe") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, AgentLineage, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has "System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData" and CommandLine has "Unprotect" and CommandLine has "FromBase64String"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| extend AgentLineage = iff(ParentProcessName has_any ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, AgentLineage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DPAPI Browser Credential Decryption via PowerShell (GStack browse skill)
id: 6f1d2a94-8c3b-4a11-9e0f-7d2c5b4a1e33
description: Detects the GStack /browse skill's PowerShell that calls DPAPI ProtectedData.Unprotect on a base64 blob to decrypt Chromium browser credentials, observed running under Claude Code/Cursor and equally used for real browser-credential theft.
references:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe) @CommandLine:(*ProtectedData* AND *Unprotect* AND *FromBase64String*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/System\.Security\.Cryptography\.ProtectedData/i
| CommandLine=/Unprotect/i
| CommandLine=/FromBase64String/i
| agent := if(ParentBaseFileName=/(claude|cursor|codex|node)\.exe/i, "ai-agent", "other")
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, agent, ImageFileName, CommandLine])

Windows Credential Manager enumeration via cmdkey /list under coding agent AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts cmdkey.exe /list — Claude Code was observed enumerating everything Windows Credential Manager holds. Rare in normal user space; the AI-agent parent lineage is surfaced to separate benign agent recon from an attacker's credential survey. Rationale: cmdkey.exe /list is the literal command Sophos attributed to Claude Code enumerating Credential Manager; it is uncommon enough in user space to hunt broadly while tagging agent lineage for fast triage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1555.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin auditing saved RDP / network credentials with cmdkey /list
  • Logon or provisioning scripts that inventory stored credentials
  • MDM/endpoint-management agents enumerating credential entries
  • A developer's coding agent legitimately checking cached credentials before an automation task
  • IT troubleshooting of Credential Manager / SSO issues
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain — a claude.exe/cursor.exe ancestor plus a developer user strongly implies benign agent recon; an interactive shell under a service or unexpected user warrants escalation. 2) Contain: if paired with credential decryption or exfil, isolate the host and rotate any credentials visible in Credential Manager for that user. 3) Hunt: search the same host/session for DPAPI browser decrypt (UC1), LOLBin downloads, and outbound connections to determine if enumeration led to use.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "cmdkey.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/list"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend AgentLineage = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, AgentLineage
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmdkey.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/list"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| extend AgentLineage = iff(ParentProcessName has_any ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, AgentLineage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

certutil-blocked-then-bitsadmin LOLBin download pivot on same host AIDelivery High
Correlates a certutil urlcache download and a bitsadmin /transfer download on the same host within a short window — the 'retry-when-blocked' pivot Sophos flagged (OpenAI Codex fetched a python.org installer with certutil, was blocked, switched to bitsadmin). The two-tool pivot is far higher signal than either LOLBin alone. Rationale: Encodes the article's exact pivot: certutil -urlcache -split download (rule Lateral_1b) blocked, then bitsadmin /transfer (rule Exec_5a); requiring BOTH LOLBins on one host in 10m is the 'live-attacker vs static script' discriminator Sophos calls out, cutting the FP rate of either LOLBin alone. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1105 T1197
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer's coding agent (Codex/Claude) fetching a real installer from python.org and retrying with a different tool when blocked — the exact benign case in the article
  • Admin scripts that download with certutil and fall back to bitsadmin on failure
  • SCCM/BITS deployments alongside certutil cert operations
  • Software build pipelines pulling dependencies via multiple utilities
  • Legit certutil -urlcache cache-clearing runs coinciding with an unrelated BITS transfer
Suppression filter
| where not (CertCmd has_any ("python.org","aka.ms","microsoft.com") and BitsCmd has_any ("python.org","aka.ms","microsoft.com") and CertParent in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe") and BitsParent in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract both command lines and the download URLs; a signed installer from python.org/vendor CDNs under an agent parent is likely benign, an unknown/low-reputation host is not. 2) Contain: if the fetched target is untrusted, quarantine the downloaded file, block the destination, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check what executed the downloaded payload next and whether the same host also shows credential access (UC1/UC2) or startup persistence (UC4).
let window = 10m;
let certutil = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "certutil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("urlcache","-split","http")
    | project CertTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, CertCmd=ProcessCommandLine, CertParent=InitiatingProcessFileName;
let bits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "bitsadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/transfer"
    | project BitsTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, BitsCmd=ProcessCommandLine, BitsParent=InitiatingProcessFileName;
certutil
| join kind=inner bits on DeviceId
| where BitsTime between (CertTime .. CertTime + window)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project CertTime, BitsTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', BitsTime, CertTime), DeviceName, AccountName, CertCmd, BitsCmd, CertParent, BitsParent
| order by CertTime desc
let window = 10m;
let certutil = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "\\certutil.exe"
    | where CommandLine has_any ("urlcache","-split","http")
    | project CertTime=TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CertCmd=CommandLine, CertParent=ParentProcessName;
let bits = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "\\bitsadmin.exe"
    | where CommandLine has "/transfer"
    | project BitsTime=TimeGenerated, Computer, BitsCmd=CommandLine, BitsParent=ParentProcessName;
certutil
| join kind=inner bits on Computer
| where BitsTime between (CertTime .. CertTime + window)
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project CertTime, BitsTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', BitsTime, CertTime), Computer, SubjectUserName, CertCmd, BitsCmd, CertParent, BitsParent
| order by CertTime desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@Image:(*\certutil.exe OR *\CertUtil.exe OR *\CERTUTIL.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*urlcache* OR *-split*)) OR (@Image:(*\bitsadmin.exe OR *\BitsAdmin.exe OR *\BITSADMIN.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*/transfer*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(certutil|bitsadmin)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/urlcache|-split|\/transfer/i
| tool := if(ImageFileName=/certutil/i, "certutil", "bitsadmin")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=[count(field=tool, distinct=true, as=tool_count), collect([CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])])
| tool_count >= 2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="certutil.exe" AND (Processes.process="*urlcache*" OR Processes.process="*-split*")) OR (Processes.process_name="bitsadmin.exe" AND Processes.process="*/transfer*") by _time span=10m Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | stats dc(process_name) as tool_count values(process_name) as tools values(process) as cmdlines values(parent_process_name) as parents min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by dest user | where tool_count>=2 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="certutil.exe" AND (Processes.process="*urlcache*" OR Processes.process="*-split*")) OR (Processes.process_name="bitsadmin.exe" AND Processes.process="*/transfer*") by _time span=10m Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | stats dc(process_name) as tool_count values(process_name) as tools values(process) as cmdlines values(parent_process_name) as parents min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by dest user | where tool_count>=2 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Startup-folder script drop via PowerShell (Cursor persistence pattern) AIInstallation Medium
Detects PowerShell creating a script (.vbs/.ps1/.bat/.cmd/.js/.lnk) in the per-user Startup folder — the persistence rule Cursor tripped when it dropped Launch-EZConvert-ConsoleOnly.vbs. Writing to Startup outside a trusted installer is flagged on sight; the agent-parent lineage separates benign build helpers from real autorun implants. Rationale: Anchors on the exact persistence behavior (rule Persist_2a) and path Sophos reported for Cursor — a script written to \Start Menu\Programs\Startup\ by PowerShell — which is high-signal because trusted installers don't use PowerShell to seed Startup. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A coding agent (Cursor/Claude) legitimately creating a launcher script in Startup for a dev tool
  • Legitimate application installers that seed Startup via a PowerShell post-install step
  • User-authored login automation dropped into Startup
  • Configuration-management tooling (DSC/Intune scripts) writing startup shortcuts
  • Backup/sync software restoring a previously-present Startup script
Suppression filter
| where not (AgentLineage == "AI coding agent" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("EZConvert","build","dev"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped file's contents and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine; a benign build helper under cursor.exe differs sharply from an obfuscated launcher or one calling out to the internet. 2) Contain: if malicious, delete the Startup artifact, kill the persistence, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same PowerShell session for credential access (UC1/UC2) and LOLBin downloads (UC3), and sweep other hosts for the same Startup filename.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".ps1" or FileName endswith ".bat" or FileName endswith ".cmd" or FileName endswith ".js" or FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| extend AgentLineage = iff(InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("cursor.exe","claude.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, AgentLineage
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("vbs","ps1","bat","cmd","js","lnk")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Claude Code launched with --dangerously-skip-permissions guardrail bypass AIExploitation High
Hunts any process invoked with Claude Code's --dangerously-skip-permissions flag, which Anthropic's own docs warn against and which lets the agent run without per-action approval. Sophos observed the credential-access activity running under this mode; it is a high-fidelity configuration-risk signal admins are told to block via managed settings. Rationale: The literal flag --dangerously-skip-permissions is a verbatim, unambiguous article string; it is essentially never present in legitimate managed environments, making it a clean policy-violation alert that also scopes which agent runs bypass approval. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer intentionally running Claude Code headless in a local sandbox or throwaway VM
  • CI/CD or container automation that runs the agent unattended with the flag by design
  • Security team reproducing the Sophos scenario in a lab
  • Documentation/demo of the flag being run once
  • Power user who accepted the risk on a personal dev box
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user and host; confirm whether the agent then performed credential access (UC1/UC2) or downloads (UC3) in the same session. 2) Contain: enforce Anthropic managed settings to disable --dangerously-skip-permissions fleet-wide and, on corporate-data hosts, revoke the agent's blanket credential-store access. 3) Hunt: pull all hosts where the flag has appeared to gauge exposure and correlate with credential-touching detections to prioritize which sessions to investigate first.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--dangerously-skip-permissions"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "--dangerously-skip-permissions"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

Protecting Microsoft at AI speed: How SFI proactively hardens our cloud

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-08 4 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

At Microsoft we encompass these security requirements, along with threat knowledge, and operational frameworks in our Secure Future Initiative (SFI), to guide what a well-defended cloud service looks like. But defining the requirements is only the start. Meeting the requirements means continuously evaluating our live services against them, at AI speed. The post Protecting Microsoft at AI speed: How SFI proactively hardens our cloud appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1190 T1528 T1566
